Let  
\[
\delta=\alpha+\beta-2\gamma>0,\qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.
\]

Using polar coordinates \(x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta\),

\[
|x+y|=r|\cos\theta+\sin\theta|,\qquad |x-y|=r|\cos\theta-\sin\theta|,
\]
so the expression becomes
\[
F(r,\theta)=r^{\alpha+\beta-2\gamma}
|\cos\theta+\sin\theta|^\alpha
|\cos\theta-\sin\theta|^\beta
=r^\delta
|\cos\theta+\sin\theta|^\alpha
|\cos\theta-\sin\theta|^\beta .
\]

If \(\alpha,\beta\ge 0\), the angular factor is bounded, since
\[
|\cos\theta+\sin\theta|\le \sqrt2,\qquad
|\cos\theta-\sin\theta|\le \sqrt2.
\]
Hence
\[
0\le F(r,\theta)\le (\sqrt2)^{\alpha+\beta}r^\delta \to 0
\]
because \(\delta>0\). Therefore, under the usual assumption \(\alpha,\beta\ge 0\), the limit exists and equals \(0\).

If \(\alpha,\beta\) are allowed to be negative, the condition \(\alpha+\beta-2\gamma>0\) alone is not sufficient. For example, take
\[
\alpha=1,\qquad \beta=-1,\qquad \gamma=-\frac12.
\]
Then \(\alpha+\beta-2\gamma=1>0\), and
\[
F(r,\theta)=r\,\frac{|\cos\theta+\sin\theta|}{|\cos\theta-\sin\theta|}.
\]
Along \(\theta=0\), \(F=r\to0\). But along \(\theta=\frac\pi4-r\),
\[
F=r\,\frac{\cos r}{\sin r}\to1.
\]
Thus the limit does not exist in general without nonnegativity of \(\alpha,\beta\).

\[
\boxed{\text{If }\alpha,\beta\ge0,\text{ the limit exists and equals }0;\text{ the given inequality alone is not sufficient otherwise.}}
\]
